title: Week 2 & 3 - Concurrency
content: - Every user thread is mapped to a kernel thread and the OS has its own kernel threads. These kernel threads are the unit of scheuduling in the OS. # How does the OS/CPU knows to switch threads? ## Interrupts Interrupts can be either internal or external. - **Internal Interrupts**: Caused by executing instructions. Can be either a fault (dividing by 0) or a trap instruction to initiate a system call. - **External Interrupts**: Caused by hardware devices needing attention. The *Programmable Interrupt Controller (PIC)* prioritizes interrupts and specifies correct interrupt handler. To handle an interrupt: - The CPU stops the currently running program and gives control to the relevant handler within the Interrupt Descriptor Table - The handler saves the current state of the running program - The handler executes - Depending on the interrupt, the handler will restore or halt the running program. ## Context Switching Happens when we receive a system clock interrupt or a system call trap. The OS handles this by: 1. Suspending the execution of the running thread 2. Saving it's execution context 3. Changing the thread's state to ready or waiting 4. Electing a new thread from the ones in the ready state 5. Changing its state to running 6. Restoring that thread's execution context 7. Resuming that thread's execution ### Where does the OS keep this information? The OS keeps track of state and execution context of threads using **Thread Control Blocks** and it maintains a collection of TCB queues. The OS will have one TCB queue for all ready threads and one for each type of blocking IO. - *State*: Whether a thread is ready, running or waiting - *Execution Context*: The registers, stack and heap of a thread # Synchronization ## What constitutes a critical section? 1. Mutual Exclusion If one thread is in the critical section then no other thread is. 2. Progress - If thread T is not in the critical section, then T cannot prevent another thread from entering critical section. - A thread in the critical section will eventually leave it. 3. Bounded Waiting - If some thread T is waiting on the critical section, then T will eventually enter the critical section 4. Performance - The overhead of entering and exiting the critical section is small with respect to the work being done within it ## Locks / Mutex A data structure that supports three methods at minimum: 1. `acquire`: waits until the mutex is unlocked 2. `release`: unlocks the mutex allowing a waiting thread to enter the critical section 3. `init`: creates an unlocked mutex ## Condition Variables A data structure that supports three operations: - `cond_wait(cond, lock)`: Given we are holding the lock when calling `cond_wait()`, it unlocks the lock and sleeps until cond is signaled then re-acquires the lock before resuming execution - `cond_signal(cond)`: signal the condition variable `cond` to wake up the next thread - `cond_broadcast(cond)`: signal the condition cond to wake up all threads ## Deadlock When one thread is trying to acquire a resource held by another thread and vice versa. Neither can make progress. Four conditions for deadlocks: - Mutual exclusion - Circular wait - No pre-emption - Hold and wait ### How to avoid deadlocks? - Make sure everyone acquires resources in the same order (make circular wait impossible) - Detect circles and break them (e.g. kill one thread) ## Semaphores Another data structure with an integer variable $R$, a queue and two operations: - `sem_wait(sem_t *s)` - Decrements the value of the semaphore by 1 - Wait in a queue if the value of semaphore is negative - `sem_post(sem_t *s)` - Increment the value R of the semaphore by one # Implementing Synchronization Primitives When implementing synchronization primitives, we have to worry about external interrupts and context switches. Consider the basic spin lock example: ```C struct lock { int held = 0; } void acquire(struct lock *lock) { while (lock->held); // What if a context switch happens right here? // Between two threads that are both trying to acquire the same lock lock->held = 1; } void release (struct lock *lock) { lock->held = 0; } ``` The solution is the `test-and-set` x86 CPU instruction that atomically writes to the memory location and returns the old value in a single indivisible step. - The caller is responsible for testing if the operation has succeeded or not # CPU Scheduling ## Scheuduling Metrics - **Throughput**: The number of threads that complete per unit time - **Turnaround time**: Time for a thread to complete - **Response time**: Time between waiting to ready transition and ready to running transition. These are affected by the CPU utilization and the waiting time. The importance of a metric depends on the system and job type. - **Batch Systems care about job throughput and turnaround time** - **Interactive systems care about response time** *Systems are often optimized for average response time or average turnaround time.* ### No Starvation as a Requirement **Starvation**: When a thread can't make progress because some other thread holds the resource it desires. - Can either be a side effect of synchronization or scheuduling semantics. ## Algorithms See OSTEP Chapter 7 for non-bolded terms. - FCFS = FIFO - SJF = Shortest-Job-First - No presumption - Treats the scheduler as an oracle that predict job length - Round-Robin: Has a FIFO queue of jobs. Each job is given a quantum and runs that duration or until it yields at which point it gets moved to end of FIFO queue. - Quantum is typically between 1-100 ms ### **SRTF = Shortest-Remaining-Time-First** If a new thread arrives CPU burst length less than time of current executing thread, preempt the current running thread. - Better for wait and turnaround time. - *Allows starvation* ### **Multilevel Queue** Associate a priority with each thread and execute highest priority thread first. If same priority, do RR. - Starvation of low priority threads is prevented by changing the priority over time - For ex, increasing priority as a function of waiting time - Deciding priority, keep track of thread CPU usage. - Initial priorities are high. We assume they are interactive. - Reduce priorities of threads with high CPU usage #### Priority Inversion and Donation In a MLQ, a high-priority job `H` can be forced to wait on a lower priority job if that lower priority job holds a synchronization primitive needed by `H`. This is **priority inversion**. It's when a higher priority thread is forced to wait on a lower priority thread. The fix is **priority donation**. The higher priority thread will donate some of it's priority to the lower priority thread. ### MLFQ Has 5 rules BUT extremely similar to MLQ: 1. If Priority(A) > Priority(B), A runs 2. If Priority(A) = Priority(B), A & B run in round-robin fashion using the queue's quantum 3. When a job enters the system, it is placed at the highest priority 4. Once a job uses up its time allotment at a given level, its priority is reduced 5. After some time period S, move all the jobs in the system to the topmost queue
